name: Varley's Green
lede: Varley's Green is a dark, muted olive green, one of the nineteenth-century "mixed greens" sold ready-made to artists alongside the related [[hooker-s-green|Hooker's Green]], and no book we hold names which Varley it honors.

sections.title: A mixed green, an unnamed Varley
sections.body:
Field's 1835 treatise groups Varley's Green with Hooker's Green as examples of "mixed greens," blends of a blue and a yellow sold to artists as particular hues rather than single pigments [1]. The Pigment Compendium repeats this pairing, noting that Salter's 1869 revision of Field no longer mentioned the pigment, and that it is similar to a mix of Prussian or Antwerp blue with gamboge [1][2]. Several English watercolourists and theorists carried the Varley name in this period, most notably the landscape painter John Varley (1778-1842), but no book we hold states that the green is named for him specifically [3].

Ridgway catalogued the color in his 1912 standards, on plate XVIII, hue 31 prime [4].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: Measured in LCH terms it is lightness 42, chroma 14, hue 134 degrees, a dark, low-saturation green [5]. Its nearest library neighbor is [[empire-green|Empire Green]], about 2.9 units away, with [[yew-green|Yew Green]] close behind [5]. Next to [[hunter-green|Hunter green]] it reads as the duller, more olive one [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this green, as photographed, in 400 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.7 percent, including Berthe Morisot's 1873 *Reading* and Gauguin's 1899 still life [6]. The earliest dated match is Lorenzo di Credi's 1400 *Virgin and Child*, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [6]. These are computed color matches on aged, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [6].
